title: Allah heard her
hook: Allah heard the woman who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and a ruling came (58:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Hadid: iron, strength sent down as a trust, and your line, strength sent down. Today, a surah named for a woman.

In a small room in Medina, a woman is speaking with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, low and urgent. Her husband, in anger, has said an old Arabian phrase to her: you are to me like my mother's back. By custom, that left a wife in limbo: not divorced, so she couldn't remarry, and not a wife, so he wouldn't come near her. She has children, and she's getting older. She argues her case. In a corner of the same house, the Prophet's wife 'A'isha can't even make out the words.

The reports name her Khawla bint Tha'laba, and her husband Aws ibn as-Samit. She pleaded, and she complained to God. And the surah that came down opens with her. Pickthall: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah." Qad sami'a Allah: God has heard. The surah is named for her: Al-Mujadila, she who disputes, she who pleads her case. A whole surah, named for a woman who argued. The next verses settle the matter. Saying that phrase doesn't make a wife into a mother; it's a wrong and false thing to say. A man who says it and wants to return must make amends first: free a slave, or if he can't, fast two months in a row, or if he can't, feed sixty poor people. The custom that trapped women was ended. And 'A'isha's reaction is the part people remember. The reports preserve her words: blessed is the One whose hearing takes in every voice. The woman was speaking to the Prophet in a corner of my house, and I couldn't hear what she said, and God heard her from above the seven heavens. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't scold her for arguing. It records her disputing and her complaint, and answers both. A voice too low for the next room was heard, and the answer became law for everyone after her.
screen: `KHAWLA PLEADS HER CASE.` · `QAD SAMI'A ALLAH: GOD HAS HEARD.` · `AN OLD CUSTOM ENDED.` · `HEARING THAT TAKES IN EVERY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been quietly unhappy about but haven't said, at home, at work, with a friend, and picture Khawla, low-voiced and steady. Shape what you need into one calm, clear sentence, no blame, just the truth of it; if you pray, bring it to God first, as she did.
Al-Mujadila: she who disputes, the surah named for Khawla, whose complaint to the Prophet, God says, he heard. Today's word.
Your line: she was heard. The week ran from the water you drink and the purified, through Al-Hadid's nearness, soft hearts, play and iron, to Khawla's quiet voice. Day six hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Khawla bint Tha'laba as an example of a woman whose plea was answered in the Qur'an; Islamic law treats zihar as forbidden and sets an expiation before a husband who said it may return to his wife.

original.note: Arabic: God has heard. The first words of Surah Al-Mujadila.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legal verse about marriage.
what it means: a woman's quiet plea, heard and answered, ending a custom that trapped wives.
what a scholar hears: zihar ('like my mother's back') ruled false in 58:2, with kaffara in 58:3–4; 'A'isha's words appear in Bukhari (Kitab at-Tawhid, ta'liq), an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.
recall: a gift, as in Allah's giving

chat.says: Why is a whole surah named after a woman who argued with the Prophet?
options: God heard her plea; the surah answers it and never scolds her for arguing.
It's meant as a warning to women not to argue with men in authority.
She was honored because she memorized the surah first.
chat.meaning: 58:1: Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee. The verse records her pleading and her complaint, and answers both.
